newsitem.title: USA: U.S. credibility at stake on arms treaty - Albright.
newsitem.headline: U.S. credibility at stake on arms treaty - Albright.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Friday that the Chemical Weapons Convention was "made in America" and the United States risked losing credibility if the Senate failed to ratify it.

"Make no mistake, the Chemical Weapons Convention is in the best interests of the United States. In fact the CWC has 'made in America' written all over it," she said in a speech at Houston's Rice University.
Conservative Republicans in the Senate say the 1993 treaty, which bans production, stockpiling and use of poison gas, is flawed, and are holding up its ratification.
Albright noted that the treaty was negotiated under former President George Bush, a Republican, and endorsed by his Republican predecessor Ronald Reagan.
If the treaty opponents had their way, she said, the United States would lose the right to administer the treaty and risk the loss of hundreds of millions of dollars in chemical export sales.

And, she said, "we would lose credibility in negotiating arms reduction agreements generally, because our ability to deliver in the Senate what we have proposed at the bargaining table would be undermined, for reasons that friends and allies around the world would find very difficult to understand."

Clinton, speaking in his annual State of the Union speech before Congress, called ratification of the treaty "a new test of leadership." He added: "It will make our troops safer from chemical attack. It will help us to fight terrorism."
The Clinton administration wants the Senate to approve the 1993 treaty by April 29. If Washington does not ratify it by then, it will have no say in the administration of the ban.

"We have no more important obligations -- especially in the wake of what we now know about the Gulf War," Clinton said, referring to reports of contamination from Iraqi chemical weapons when U.S. forces blew up Iraqi bunkers.
